title: The Messy, Majestic Vote
markdown:
The University Common Room, usually a hush of teacups and footnotes, crackled. Autumn pressed its face to the windows. Tonight the Society of Arcane Arts would vote, an event as solemn as finding the last biscuit in the tin, which was, in fact, the subject. Ancient, possibly sentient biscuit tins were to be allocated. Careers had been built on less.

Elara the hedgehog, assistant to Professor Quillsby, had spent weeks on this night. Her plan was a silent symphony: ferns at measured intervals, a seating chart that could have been framed, name cards that did not dare to curl. Her quills hummed. Nothing, she had decided, would be left to interpretation.

Then an earthquake of whispers. Professor Ceredig, society president, a badger whose frown could curdle milk, barked from the hearth end.

“We must reassign the voting delegates! Swiftly!”

Elara’s ferns quaked. The chart she loved was about to be tossed like a leaf. A knot tightened. My perfect plan, she thought, spines suddenly feeling like a public exhibition. It is all going to fall apart.

Finn the stoat arrived like a comet of good intentions. He saw not doom but enhancement.

“Elara, my dear! You look overwhelmed! All this symmetry is dreadfully dull. We need dynamism!”

Before she could squeak a protocol, he was a whirlwind, nudging delegates into groupings he deemed interesting. A wizard famous for explosive pronouncements landed beside a gnome who brewed chamomile so calm it could flatten a riot. The tension did not leave. It changed flavour, from dull hum to anxious twang.

“Finn, please! The alignment! The protocol!”

“Alignment?” Finn beamed and held up a tarnished silver tray. On it, precarious as a joke, sat a delegate’s spectacles. In his rush he had arranged the seats so the only reflection was the sneer of a gargoyle statue. “It needs a focal point! Something to capture the eye!”

Professor Ceredig cleared his throat, gravel in a mill. “This is hardly conducive to a fair vote. Conduct it properly, or the Society’s reputation for fairness will be tatters.”

A murmur moved the menagerie of academe: bewilderment, suppressed amusement, the particular silence of people who have lost their assigned chairs.

Elara’s quills drooped. Finn, still radiant, decided the podium lacked gravitas. He draped it in discarded velvet curtains and nearly sent the ancient quill-holder—the vessel of the society’s most sacred pen—tumbling. “Regal flair!” he announced, as the stand wobbled like a guilty conscience.

“Finn, stop!” Elara’s voice cracked. She wanted to tidy the entire century. “This is not flair. It is knowing who is supposed to be where, and why.”

“But everyone knows,” Finn insisted, rearranging dusty scrolls. “They’re here to vote. That’s the main thing.”

Ceredig sighed the sigh of presidents. “Elara. Perhaps you might do our enthusiastic friend the honour of explaining why his improvements are, to put it mildly, problematic.”

She looked. Finn balanced a feather on an owl delegate’s nose. The seating made bewildered silence and uneasy chatter. The gargoyle mocked from the tray. Burnt tea hung in the air like a bad footnote.

This was the middle of the night, the test of her old pattern: if she could not keep the chart, she could at least keep quiet and die of neatness. The vote mattered now because the tins would go to whoever shouted through the velvet. She chose, instead, the unplanned sentence.

“It is not just about being here,” Elara said, and the clarity surprised her. “It is about feeling respected. Feeling heard. Right now nobody feels heard. They feel shuffled. And the thing we have all been too afraid to admit is how truly messy this has become.”

Hush. Finn froze mid-feather. The owl stirred. Elara’s quills stood as if they had remembered their job.

Ceredig looked from hedgehog to stoat, then at the room, and a slow smile arrived without permission. “Well said. Finn, your enthusiasm is remarkable. Elara’s observation is what we need.”

He turned to the crowd. “Let us acknowledge the rather large elephant—or rather, the flustered hedgehog and the misguided stoat. We are in charming disarray. The biscuit tins are paramount. So we reset. Sometimes the path to order is admitting the beautiful baffling mess we have so enthusiastically made.”

The evening shifted as if a window had been opened. Finn, gleam of understanding now, helped gather scattered voting slips.

“Perhaps next time we plan the seating together,” he mused. “A bit of your order. A bit of my flair.”

Elara found herself smiling. “Perhaps, Finn. That might just work.”

Delegates, sharing glances and the odd chuckle, found their proper places. The vote proceeded without rigid perfection and with a communal warmth born of having said the obvious out loud. The ferns, slightly askew, were left askew. The gargoyle, deprived of its exclusive audience, went back to being stone. On the podium the sacred quill sat in its holder, uncurtained, and Professor Ceredig’s frown, if not gone, had at least stopped curdling the milk.
audience: young adults aged 16-18, teen anthology entry
